---
title: "🎓 Tutorial: the Northeast Pacific (FAO area 67) from zero to a report"
description: >
  A complete worked example: get the FAO data, analyse FAO major fishing area 67 (Alaska, Canada
  and the US west coast) step by step with every function of the package, read and interpret each
  chart, find the files the package saves, and export the assessment report as Word, LaTeX and PDF.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
source("_setup.R")
# CMSY++ charts and results made beforehand by data-raw/tutorial67_figures.R (JAGS is not
# available when the site is built)
fig_dir <- normalizePath(file.path("figures", "tutorial-67", "en"))
show_png <- function(file) {
  knitr::asis_output(sprintf('<figure class="fao-figure"><img src="%s" alt="%s" loading="lazy"></figure>',
                             knitr::image_uri(file.path(fig_dir, file)), file))
}
pct <- function(x, digits = 1) paste0(formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits), "%")
mt <- function(x, digits = 1) paste(formatC(x / 1e6, format = "f", digits = digits), "million t")
# yearly catch of the rows of `data` that match `keep`
yearly <- function(data, keep) tapply(data$Production[keep], data$Year[keep], sum, na.rm = TRUE)
```

```{r data-source, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
data_source()
```

This tutorial walks through a complete assessment of one FAO major fishing area, the
**Northeast Pacific (FAO area 67)**, from an empty R session to a finished report. Area 67
stretches from the eastern Bering Sea and the Gulf of Alaska along the coasts of Canada and the
United States down to northern California (40° N). The tutorial uses almost every function of the
package, in the order you would use them in your own work, and explains **what each chart shows,
how to read it and what it says about the area**. If you have never used the package, read it from
top to bottom and run the code as you go; if you know the package, use the table of contents to
jump to the step you need.

Area 67 is a good teaching example because its history is written clearly in the data: for twenty
years the fleets of Japan and the USSR took a large part of its catch, until the United States and
Canada extended their fishery limits to 200 nautical miles in 1977 and the catch passed to their
own fleets. It is dominated by one species, the Alaska pollock, it holds a famous case of
overfishing (the Pacific ocean perch) and the salmon fisheries of the North Pacific, and its data
are among the best of all FAO areas. Every number in the text below is computed from the data when
the page is built, so it matches the charts.

| Step | What you do | Functions |
|---|---|---|
| [1](#prepare) | Prepare R, a project folder and the settings | `fao_settings()`, `fao_font()` |
| [2](#data) | Get the FAO data, know its version, save your own copy | `check_fao_update()`, `download_fao_data()`, `load_fao_data()`, `fao_data_info()` |
| [3](#area) | The catch of the area: trend, stages, share of the world | `fishing_area_data()` |
| [4](#species) | The main species | `fishing_area_species()` |
| [5](#countries) | The main countries | `fishing_area_country()` |
| [6](#one) | One species, one country | `species_country()`, `country_species()`, `country_analysis()` |
| [7](#status) | Composition, stock status, trends and shifts | `species_group_composition()`, `stock_status()`, `peak_trend()`, `regime_shift()`, `area_overview()` |
| [8](#quality) | Data quality, diversity and fleets | `data_quality()`, `diversity_concentration()`, `country_group_summary()`, `coastal_distant()` |
| [9](#literature) | Methods from the literature | `catch_shocks()`, `collapse_analysis()`, `catch_synchrony()`, `pelagic_demersal()`, `distant_water_profile()` |
| [10](#temperature) | Species traits and temperature | `fishbase_match()`, `fao_area_sst()`, `mean_temperature_catch()` |
| [11](#cmsy) | Stock assessment of the main species | `cmsy_setup()`, `cmsy_area()` |
| [12](#report) | The report in Word, LaTeX and PDF (with TinyTeX) | `fao_report()`, `tinytex::install_tinytex()` |
| [13](#files) | Where everything is saved and how to get it back | |

::: callout-note
**How the charts are explained.** Under each chart, "🔎 How to read it" describes the axes,
colours and lines, and "What it shows for area 67" gives the result. Charts describe the
**reported catch**: they say what was landed and reported to FAO, not how many fish are in the
sea. Keep that in mind for every conclusion.
:::

## 1. 🧰 Prepare {#prepare}

Install the package once, with all the packages it uses (see [🚀 Get started](get-started.html)
for details), then load it at the start of every session:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("Linbojun99/faofishingreport", dependencies = TRUE)
```

```{r}
library(faofishingreport)
```

**Work in a project folder.** Every function saves its charts and tables in the *working
directory* (the folder `getwd()` returns). Create one folder per assessment, e.g. with an RStudio
project, or set it yourself:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
dir.create("~/fao67", showWarnings = FALSE)
setwd("~/fao67")
getwd()
```

**Choose the settings once for the session** with `fao_settings()`: the language of the charts,
their style and the output formats. Call it without arguments to see the current settings.

```{r}
fao_settings(lang = "en", theme = "classic", dpi = 100, pptx = FALSE)
```

| Setting | Here | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `lang` | `"en"` | Chart text and names in English; `"zh"` Chinese; `"both"` both |
| `theme` | `"classic"` | Chart style (see [🎨 Customise](customise.html)) |
| `dpi` | `100` | Resolution of the PNG files (300 for print) |
| `pptx` | `FALSE` | `TRUE` also saves every chart as an editable PowerPoint file |

The chart font is chosen for your system (`fao_font()` shows it): SimSun on Windows, Songti SC on
macOS, Noto Serif CJK SC on Linux, so that Chinese names display.

## 2. 💾 Get the data {#data}

### 2.1 Check for the newest FAO release

FAO publishes the Global Capture Production statistics once a year. The package comes with a
recent release; `check_fao_update()` compares it with the newest one online, and
`download_fao_data()` downloads and converts a release (about 6 MB, usually under a minute):

```{r, eval = FALSE}
check_fao_update()     # newest release online vs. the data on your computer
download_fao_data()    # download the newest release (only when FAO publishes a new one)
```

### 2.2 Load the data and know which release you use

`load_fao_data()` returns the newest release available on your computer (downloaded, or else the
one bundled with the package), one row per country, species item, area and year:

```{r}
fao <- load_fao_data()
dim(fao)
show_table(fao[fao$FAO.major.fishing.area..Name. == "Pacific, Northeast" & fao$Year == 2024, ], n = 5)
```

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Country..Name.` | Reporting country (FAO English name) |
| `ASFIS.species..Name.` | FAO species item (a species, a genus, a family or a group such as "Marine fishes nei", *nei* = not elsewhere included) |
| `FAO.major.fishing.area..Name.` | FAO major fishing area |
| `Year`, `Production` | Year and catch in tonnes live weight |
| `Production.Type` | How the value was obtained: reported by the country, estimated by FAO, ... |

**Always record the release you used**: FAO revises past years in every release, so a report must
say which one it is based on. `fao_data_info()` gives the release, its dates, the download link
and a citation:

```{r}
info <- fao_data_info()
info
```

### 2.3 Where the data are kept

Downloaded releases are kept in the data folder of the package, `fao_data_dir()`, and used again
in every session. To share one folder between computers or a team, set the environment variable
`FAOFISHINGREPORT_DATA_DIR` in `~/.Renviron` (see [💾 FAO data](data.html)). Your own copies of
the data of an area can be saved like any R object:

```{r}
fao_data_dir()
area67_raw <- fao[fao$FAO.major.fishing.area..Name. == "Pacific, Northeast", ]
saveRDS(area67_raw, "area67_data.rds")                 # for R: readRDS("area67_data.rds")
write.csv(area67_raw, "area67_data.csv", row.names = FALSE, fileEncoding = "UTF-8")   # for Excel
```

## 3. 🌊 The catch of the area {#area}

`fishing_area_data()` takes the name of an FAO major area, keeps its data, and draws the total
catch with its stages and the share of the area in the world marine catch:

```{r, figures = "fishing_trend|fishing_percentage"}
NEP <- fishing_area_data("Pacific, Northeast")
area67 <- NEP$area_data
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
total <- tapply(area67$Production, area67$Year, sum, na.rm = TRUE)
last_year <- max(area67$Year)
peak_year <- as.integer(names(which.max(total)))
periods <- NEP$coefs_data
world <- tapply(fao$Production[fao$FAO.major.fishing.area..Name. %in% fao_area_sst()$area_en],
                fao$Year[fao$FAO.major.fishing.area..Name. %in% fao_area_sst()$area_en], sum, na.rm = TRUE)
share <- 100 * total / world[names(total)]
```

**`fishing_trend.png`: total catch and its stages**

🔎 *How to read it.* The grey area is the yearly catch of the area (million tonnes). The vertical
dashed lines are **breakpoints**: years in which the mean catch changes, found with the
Bai-Perron test (`strucchange::breakpoints()`); a stage starts at each dashed line. The
horizontal grey segments are the mean catch of each stage.

*What it shows for area 67.* The catch rose from `r mt(total[1])` in `r min(area67$Year)` to a
peak of `r mt(max(total))` in `r peak_year`, and was `r mt(total[as.character(last_year)])` in
`r last_year`. The test finds `r nrow(periods)` stages:
`r paste0(periods$start_year, "–", periods$end_year, " (mean ", mt(periods$intercept), ")", collapse = "; ")`.
They follow the history of the fleets, which the next steps show one by one: a small catch of
salmon and herring by Canada and the United States in the 1950s; the arrival of the trawlers of
the USSR and Japan, which fished the groundfish of the Bering Sea and the Gulf of Alaska from the
1960s; and, after the 200-mile fishery limits of 1977, the growth of the fleets of the United
States to the high, steady catch of the last four decades.

**`fishing_percentage.png`: share of the world marine catch**

🔎 *How to read it.* Each point is the catch of the area as a percentage of the catch of all FAO
marine areas in that year; the red line is the mean of these shares. Inland waters are not
counted.

*What it shows for area 67.* The area took between `r pct(min(share))` and `r pct(max(share))` of
the world marine catch, `r pct(mean(share))` on average, and `r pct(share[as.character(last_year)])`
in `r last_year`. A share above its mean means the area grew faster (or declined more slowly)
than the rest of the world's oceans: here in the 1980s, when its catch reached its plateau.

::: callout-tip
`NEP` is a list: `NEP$area_data` (the data of the area, used by all the next steps),
`NEP$coefs_data` (the stages: first and last year and mean catch) and `NEP$act_world_map` (the map
data). Save it with `saveRDS(NEP, "NEP.rds")` to continue later without recomputing.
:::

## 4. 🐟 The main species {#species}

`fishing_area_species()` ranks the species items by their catch (`rank_range = 1:10`: the ten
largest), draws their catch over time and finds the stages of each:

```{r, figures = "area_species"}
sp <- fishing_area_species(area67, rank_range = 1:10)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
sp_last5 <- area67[area67$Year > last_year - 5, ]
sp5 <- sort(tapply(sp_last5$Production, sp_last5$ASFIS.species..Name., sum, na.rm = TRUE) / 5, decreasing = TRUE)
pollock_name <- "Alaska pollock(=Walleye poll.)"
pollock_share <- 100 * sum(area67$Production[area67$ASFIS.species..Name. == pollock_name]) / sum(area67$Production)
all_items <- sort(tapply(area67$Production, area67$ASFIS.species..Name., sum, na.rm = TRUE), decreasing = TRUE)
next9 <- 100 * sum(all_items[2:10]) / sum(all_items)
pop <- yearly(area67, area67$ASFIS.species..Name. == "Pacific ocean perch")
pop_peak <- as.integer(names(which.max(pop)))
herring <- yearly(area67, area67$ASFIS.species..Name. == "Pacific herring")
pink <- yearly(area67, area67$ASFIS.species..Name. == "Pink(=Humpback) salmon")
pink <- pink[as.integer(names(pink)) >= 2000]
pink_odd <- mean(pink[as.integer(names(pink)) %% 2 == 1])
pink_even <- mean(pink[as.integer(names(pink)) %% 2 == 0])
```

**`area_species.png`: the main species together**, and **`area_species_wrap.png`: one panel per
species**

🔎 *How to read them.* The first chart puts the ten species items on one scale, to compare their
size. The second gives each species its own panel and scale, so that small species are readable:
the line is the yearly catch, the dashed vertical lines and grey segments are the stages of that
species, the dashed slanted line is a linear trend, and the percentage is the share of the species
in the catch of the area over all years.

*What it shows for area 67.* Over the last five years the largest items were
`r paste0(names(sp5)[1:5], " (", mt(sp5[1:5], 2), " a year)", collapse = ", ")`.
Four patterns stand out:

- **One species dominates.** The Alaska pollock gave `r pct(pollock_share)` of all the catch of
  the area since `r min(area67$Year)`, against `r pct(next9)` for the next nine items together. What happens to the
  pollock happens to the area.
- **Boom and bust.** The Pacific ocean perch, a rockfish, went from `r mt(pop[1], 2)` in
  `r names(pop)[1]` to a peak of `r mt(max(pop), 2)` in `r names(which.max(pop))`, taken mostly by
  Soviet and Japanese trawlers, and fell to `r mt(pop[as.character(pop_peak + 10)], 2)` ten years
  later. Rockfishes grow
  slowly and live long, so they cannot sustain a heavy catch for long.
- **A fishery that faded.** The Pacific herring gave `r mt(herring[1], 2)` in `r names(herring)[1]`
  and peaked at `r mt(max(herring), 2)` in `r names(which.max(herring))`; its catch in
  `r last_year` was `r mt(herring[length(herring)], 3)`.
- **Two-year cycles.** The pink salmon lives two years, so its runs alternate: since 2000 the
  catch averaged `r mt(pink_odd, 2)` in odd years and `r mt(pink_even, 2)` in even years, the
  zigzag in its panel.

::: callout-note
Changing `rank_range` changes the species shown, e.g. `rank_range = 11:20` for the next ten.
The lines in the panels are smoothed only if `timeseries_analysis = FALSE`, which also removes
the stages.
:::

## 5. 🌎 The main countries {#countries}

`fishing_area_country()` does the same for the countries, and adds a map of their catch:

```{r, figures = "area_country"}
co <- fishing_area_country(area67, rank_range = 1:8)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
co_last5 <- tapply(sp_last5$Production, sp_last5$Country..Name., sum, na.rm = TRUE) / 5
co_last5 <- sort(co_last5, decreasing = TRUE)
usa <- yearly(area67, area67$Country..Name. == "United States of America")
japan <- yearly(area67, area67$Country..Name. == "Japan")
korea <- yearly(area67, area67$Country..Name. == "Korea, Republic of")
ussr <- yearly(area67, area67$Country..Name. == "Un. Sov. Soc. Rep.")
ahead <- names(usa)[usa > japan[names(usa)]]
overtake <- min(as.integer(ahead[as.integer(ahead) > as.integer(names(which.max(japan)))]))
usa_share <- function(year) pct(100 * usa[as.character(year)] / total[as.character(year)], 0)
last_japan <- max(as.integer(names(japan)[japan > 1000]))
by_country <- tapply(area67$Production, list(area67$Year, area67$Country..Name.), sum, na.rm = TRUE)
leader <- colnames(by_country)[apply(by_country, 1, which.max)]
names(leader) <- rownames(by_country)
lead_years <- function(country) paste(range(as.integer(names(leader))[leader == country]), collapse = "–")
canada_50s <- sum(leader[as.character(1950:1959)] == "Canada")
```

🔎 *How to read them.* As for the species: one panel per country with its stages, trend and share
of the catch over all years; the map colours each country by its total catch in the area.

*What it shows for area 67.* Over the last five years,
`r paste0(names(co_last5)[1:2], " (", pct(100 * co_last5[1:2] / sum(co_last5)), ")", collapse = " and ")`
took almost all of the catch. It was not always so. **Canada** was the largest fishing country in
`r canada_50s` years of the 1950s; the **USSR** was the largest in `r lead_years("Un. Sov. Soc. Rep.")`
(its peak: `r mt(max(ussr))` in `r names(which.max(ussr))`) and **Japan** in
`r lead_years("Japan")` (its peak: `r mt(max(japan))` in `r names(which.max(japan))`); the
**Republic of Korea** reached `r mt(max(korea))` in `r names(which.max(korea))`. The share of the **United States** was only
`r usa_share(1970)` in 1970 and `r usa_share(1980)` in 1980, then `r usa_share(1990)` in 1990 and
`r usa_share(last_year)` in `r last_year`; it has caught more than Japan every year since
`r overtake`, and Japan's last catch above 1 000 t in the area was in `r last_japan`.

This change has a clear cause. The Fishery Conservation and Management Act of the United States
(1976, in force on 1 March 1977) created a 200-mile fishery zone and gave foreign fleets only the
part of the catch that US fleets could not take; Canada extended its fishery limit to 200 miles in
the same year. In the 1980s US fishing vessels first sold their catch to foreign processing ships
at sea ("joint ventures"), then landed it at home, until foreign fishing ended. The panels of
Japan, the USSR, Korea and Poland all end in those years.

## 6. 🔍 One species, one country {#one}

### 6.1 Who catches a species: `species_country()`

```{r, figures = "Alaska_pollock"}
pollock <- species_country(area67, "Alaska pollock(=Walleye poll.)", rank_range = 1:5)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
pol <- area67[area67$ASFIS.species..Name. == pollock_name, ]
pol_peak <- function(country) {
  x <- yearly(pol, pol$Country..Name. == country)
  paste0(mt(max(x), 2), " in ", names(which.max(x)))
}
```

🔎 *How to read them.* The charts break the catch of one species item down by country: the
ranked chart and the small multiples (one panel per country, with stages), a pie chart of the
countries by period and a map. Species names must be written as in the FAO data
(`unique(area67$ASFIS.species..Name.)` lists them; `fao_translate()` gives the Chinese names).

*What it shows for area 67.* The pollock story is the story of the area in miniature. Japan
developed the fishery (peak `r pol_peak("Japan")`), followed by the USSR
(peak `r pol_peak("Un. Sov. Soc. Rep.")`) and the Republic of Korea
(peak `r pol_peak("Korea, Republic of")`). The United States caught almost no pollock before
1980; its catch rose through the joint ventures of the 1980s and has been the only large one since,
with a peak of `r pol_peak("United States of America")`.

### 6.2 What a country catches: `country_species()` and `country_analysis()`

`country_species()` breaks down the catch of one country in the area by species;
`country_analysis()` looks at the same country in **all** FAO areas, to see where it fishes:

```{r, figures = "United_States_of_America"}
usa_67 <- country_species(area67, "United States of America", rank_range = 1:10)
usa_all <- country_analysis("United States of America", rank_range = 1:10)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
us <- area67[area67$Country..Name. == "United States of America", ]
us_top <- function(years) {
  x <- us[us$Year %in% years, ]
  names(sort(tapply(x$Production, x$ASFIS.species..Name., sum), decreasing = TRUE))[1:3]
}
us_all <- fao[fao$Country..Name. == "United States of America" &
                fao$FAO.major.fishing.area..Name. %in% c("Pacific, Northeast", "Atlantic, Northwest"), ]
us_area <- tapply(us_all$Production, list(us_all$Year, us_all$FAO.major.fishing.area..Name.), sum)
us_lead <- min(as.integer(rownames(us_area))[us_area[, "Pacific, Northeast"] > us_area[, "Atlantic, Northwest"]])
```

🔎 *How to read them.* `United_States_of_America_species_*` charts: the species of the United
States in area 67. `United_States_of_Americaanalysis_*` charts: the species of the United States in
all areas, its catch by area (`United_States_of_Americayearly_area_production.png`, one line per
area) and a map of the areas where it fishes.

*What it shows.* In the 1970s the US catch in area 67 was mostly
`r paste(us_top(1970:1979), collapse = ", ")`: salmon, crabs and shrimps of the coastal fisheries.
Over the last five years it was `r paste(us_top((last_year - 4):last_year), collapse = ", ")`: the
groundfish that the foreign fleets had caught before. Across all FAO areas, area 67 has been the
largest fishing area of the United States since `r us_lead`, when it passed the Northwest
Atlantic; it now gives far more than all other areas.

## 7. 📈 Composition, stock status, trends and shifts {#status}

### 7.1 Species groups: `species_group_composition()`

```{r, figures = "group"}
groups <- species_group_composition(area67)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
gy <- as.data.frame(groups$yearly)
group_pct <- function(group, year) {
  y <- gy[gy$Year == year, ]
  pct(100 * sum(y$Tonnes[y$category %in% group]) / sum(y$Tonnes), 0)
}
```

🔎 *How to read it.* Species items are grouped into the ISSCAAP groups of FAO (e.g. "Herrings,
sardines, anchovies", "Cods, hakes, haddocks"). The stacked areas show the catch of each group,
and the `_share` chart its percentage of the catch; the largest groups are named, the others are
"Other groups".

*What it shows for area 67.* In 1950 the salmons (`r group_pct("Salmons, trouts, smelts", 1950)`)
and the herrings (`r group_pct("Herrings, sardines, anchovies", 1950)`) made up most of the catch,
and the cods, hakes and haddocks only `r group_pct("Cods, hakes, haddocks", 1950)`. The trawl
fisheries changed this within twenty years: the cods, hakes and haddocks (pollock, Pacific cod,
Pacific hake) reached `r group_pct("Cods, hakes, haddocks", 1970)` in 1970 and
`r group_pct("Cods, hakes, haddocks", last_year)` in `r last_year`, with the flatfishes second.

### 7.2 Stock status plots: `stock_status()`

```{r, figures = "stock_status"}
status <- stock_status(area67)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
st_last <- status$yearly[status$yearly$Year == last_year, ]
st_pct <- function(label, column = "stocks_pct") sum(st_last[[column]][st_last$status_label %in% label])
```

🔎 *How to read them.* Each "stock" is the catch series of one species item in the area. Every
year, a stock is classed by its catch relative to its own peak (Kleisner et al. 2013):
**developing** (before the peak, below half of it), **exploited** (above half of the peak),
**over-exploited** (after the peak, 10–50% of it), **collapsed** (after the peak, below 10%) and
**rebuilding** (back to 10–50% after a collapse). The `_stocks` chart counts stocks, the
`_catch` chart weights them by their catch.

*What it shows for area 67.* Of the `r nrow(status$stocks)` stocks, in `r last_year`
`r pct(st_pct("Collapsed"))` were collapsed and `r pct(st_pct("Over-exploited"))` over-exploited
by number. Weighted by catch the picture is very different: the collapsed stocks took only
`r pct(st_pct("Collapsed", "catch_pct"))` of the catch and the over-exploited ones
`r pct(st_pct("Over-exploited", "catch_pct"))`, while the exploited stocks, still above half of
their peak, took `r pct(st_pct("Exploited", "catch_pct"))`. Many small stocks are far below their
old peaks (some of them, like the herring, because their fisheries were closed or not wanted
any more), but the large stocks that give most of the catch are not.

::: callout-warning
**What not to conclude.** A stock status plot uses catch only. A fall in catch can come from
fewer fish, but also from less fishing, management, markets or a change in reporting (e.g. a
species reported as "nei"). Use it to ask questions, not as a stock assessment; `smooth = TRUE`
classes the 3-year running mean, which reduces the effect of single bad years.
:::

### 7.3 Peak and trend of each species: `peak_trend()`

```{r, figures = "peak_trend"}
pt <- peak_trend(area67)
show_table(pt[, c("name", "peak_year", "pct_of_peak", "growth_pct_per_year", "trend")], n = 11)
```

🔎 *How to read it.* For each of the main species: the year of its peak catch, the catch of the
last year as a percentage of that peak, the mean yearly growth over the last ten years and the
Mann-Kendall test of that trend ("up", "down" or "none" at *P* < 0.05). In area 67 the total
and the pollock are both close to their peak of the late 1980s, while the herring and the
Pacific ocean perch are far below theirs.

### 7.4 Synchronous shifts: `regime_shift()`

```{r, figures = "regime_shift"}
shifts <- regime_shift(area67)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
rs_top <- shifts$yearly[order(-shifts$yearly$n_species), ][1:3, ]
```

🔎 *How to read it.* The breakpoints of each main species are found as in step 4; the bar chart
counts, for every year, how many species changed their mean catch in that year. Years when many
species change together point to a common cause: the ocean (a regime shift), a change of
management, or a change of reporting.

*What it shows for area 67.* The years with the most simultaneous breakpoints are
`r paste0(rs_top$Year, " (", rs_top$n_species, " species)", collapse = ", ")`. The North Pacific
had well-known climate regime shifts in 1977 and 1989 (Hare and Mantua 2000), but the catch
breakpoints cluster instead in the 1980s, the years when the catch passed from foreign to US
fleets. In catch data, fleets and management often leave a larger mark than the ocean; a
breakpoint alone cannot tell which cause it was.

### 7.5 All FAO areas compared: `area_overview()`

```{r, figures = "marine_areas"}
overview <- area_overview()
```

🔎 *How to read it.* The catch of every FAO marine area over time, and their peak year and recent
trend. It places area 67 among the others: a medium-sized area with a catch that has been steady
for four decades, unlike the areas that peaked and declined.

## 8. 🔍 Data quality, diversity and fleets {#quality}

### 8.1 How good are the data? `data_quality()`

```{r, figures = "data_quality"}
quality <- data_quality(area67)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
tq <- quality$taxon_level[quality$taxon_level$Year == last_year, ]
tq$pct <- 100 * tq$Tonnes / sum(tq$Tonnes)
sq <- quality$data_status[quality$data_status$Year == last_year, ]
sq$pct <- 100 * sq$Tonnes / sum(sq$Tonnes)
```

🔎 *How to read them.* `_taxon_share`: the share of the catch identified to species, genus,
family, or only to order or higher (e.g. "Marine fishes nei"). `_status_share`: the share reported
officially by countries and the share estimated by FAO or the country.

*What it shows for area 67.* In `r last_year`, `r pct(tq$pct[tq$category == "Species"])` of the
catch was identified to species, only `r pct(tq$pct[tq$category == "Order or higher"])` to order
or higher, and `r pct(sq$pct[sq$category == "Official data"])` was official data reported by the
countries. Few areas have data this good: the species charts above describe nearly the whole
catch, and a change in a species is unlikely to be a change in reporting.

### 8.2 Diversity and concentration: `diversity_concentration()`

```{r, figures = "diversity"}
div <- diversity_concentration(area67)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
dl <- div[div$Year == last_year, ]
```

🔎 *How to read it.* Seven indicators, one per panel: the number of species items and of countries
reporting, the Shannon diversity of the species, the Herfindahl-Hirschman index (HHI) of the
species and of the countries, and the share of the five largest species and countries. The HHI
goes from near 0 (catch spread over many) to 10 000 (one takes all); above 2 500 is "highly
concentrated".

*What it shows for area 67.* In `r last_year`, `r dl$n_species` species items and
`r dl$n_countries` countries reported catch. Both indices are above 2 500: the HHI of the
countries was `r round(dl$hhi_countries)`, close to its maximum, because the United States takes
almost everything, and the HHI of the species was `r round(dl$hhi_species)`, because of the
pollock. The area has many species, but its catch depends on one country and one species.

### 8.3 Who fishes: `country_group_summary()` and `coastal_distant()`

```{r, figures = "country_income|coastal_distant"}
income <- country_group_summary(area67)
fleets <- coastal_distant(area67)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
fl <- as.data.frame(fleets$yearly)
fl_total <- tapply(fl$Tonnes, fl$Year, sum)
fl_distant <- tapply(fl$Tonnes[fl$category == "Distant-water countries"], fl$Year[fl$category == "Distant-water countries"], sum)
fl_pct <- 100 * fl_distant / fl_total[names(fl_distant)]
fl_end <- min(as.integer(names(fl_pct))[fl_pct < 1 & as.integer(names(fl_pct)) > as.integer(names(which.max(fl_pct)))])
```

🔎 *How to read them.* `country_income`: the catch by World Bank income group of the countries.
`coastal_distant`: the catch of **coastal countries** (whose territory borders the area) and of
**distant-water countries**, from the FAO area boundaries and country outlines.

*What it shows for area 67.* Nearly all the catch is taken by high-income countries; the
"not classified" part of the 1960s and 1970s is the USSR, which no longer exists. The
distant-water countries (Japan, the Republic of Korea, Poland and others) took
`r pct(fl_pct["1960"], 0)` of the catch in 1960 and up to `r pct(max(fl_pct), 0)` in
`r names(which.max(fl_pct))`; their share fell below 1% in `r fl_end` and has stayed there. Note
that the USSR and the Russian Federation count as coastal, because part of the Russian coast on the
Bering Sea borders the area: the foreign share of the catch before 1990 was even larger than the
distant-water share.

## 9. 🔬 Methods from the literature {#literature}

These analyses follow published methods; [🔬 Shocks, collapses, synchrony and fleets](literature-analyses.html)
explains each in detail.

### 9.1 Catch shocks: `catch_shocks()`

```{r, figures = "shocks"}
shocks_country <- catch_shocks(area67)
shocks_species <- catch_shocks(area67, by = "species", label = "area67_species")
```

🔎 *How to read them.* A **shock** is a year in which the catch of a series fell far below what
its recent years predicted (Cottrell et al. 2019). The bar chart gives the percentage of series
with a shock in each year; `_series` shows the series with their shocks, `_by_country` /
`_by_continent` count them by group.

*What it shows for area 67.* By country (`by = c("country", "area")`, the default), area 67 has
only `r nrow(shocks_country$series)` series, so each shock is a large percentage and the chart is
coarse. By species there are `r nrow(shocks_species$series)` series and
`r nrow(shocks_species$shocks)` shocks, a more informative picture for one area. **Choose the
series to fit the question**: countries for national food supply, species for ecology.

### 9.2 Fishery collapses: `collapse_analysis()`

```{r, figures = "collapse"}
set.seed(1)   # the comparison with random series uses random numbers
collapses <- collapse_analysis(area67)
show_table(collapses$summary)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
cs <- collapses$summary[collapses$summary$type == "collapsed", ]
```

🔎 *How to read it.* A series (one species by one country) has **collapsed** when, after its
maximum, its catch stays below a tenth of the maximum for four years (Mullon et al. 2005). The
bars count collapses by year and by the shape of the decline before them (plateau, smooth or
erratic). The function repeats the analysis on random series without trend, because random ups
and downs alone produce some "collapses" (Wilberg and Miller 2007): only the excess over that
null model is informative.

*What it shows for area 67.* `r cs$n` of the `r cs$n_series` series collapsed
(`r pct(cs$pct_of_series, 0)`), against `r pct(cs$null_pct_of_series, 0)` of the random series.
`r if (cs$pct_of_series <= cs$null_pct_of_series + 5) "That is about what random variability alone produces, so the collapses of area 67 are, as a whole, no evidence of a fishery-wide problem; look at the individual series instead." else "That is more than random variability alone produces: the excess points to declines with a common cause."`
This is why the null model matters: without it, `r pct(cs$pct_of_series, 0)` of the series "collapsed" would sound alarming.

### 9.3 Synchrony and the portfolio effect: `catch_synchrony()`

```{r, figures = "synchrony"}
sync <- catch_synchrony(area67)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
most_variable <- sync$series$series_en[which.max(sync$series$cv)]
```

🔎 *How to read them.* `_cv`: the coefficient of variation (year-to-year variability) of each
species and, in red, of the total catch. `_correlation`: how the species vary together. The
synchrony index φ is 0 when species compensate each other and 1 when they rise and fall together
(Loreau and de Mazancourt 2008).

*What it shows for area 67.* φ = `r round(sync$summary$synchrony_phi, 2)`: the total catch varies
(CV `r round(sync$summary$cv_total, 2)`) much less than its species (mean CV
`r round(sync$summary$mean_cv_series, 2)`): the species are on average
`r pct(sync$summary$portfolio_effect_pct, 0)` more variable than their total. This **portfolio
effect** means that when one species declines, others take its place. Among the main species in
the chart, the `r most_variable` is by far the most variable, the mark of its boom and bust.

### 9.4 Pelagic to demersal ratio: `pelagic_demersal()`

```{r, figures = "pelagic_demersal"}
pd <- pelagic_demersal(area67)
show_table(pd$decades[, c("period", "pd_mean", "pd_min", "pd_max")])
```

🔎 *How to read them.* P/D is the catch of small pelagic fishes divided by the catch of demersal
fishes and crustaceans (Caddy 1993; de Leiva Moreno et al. 2000), on a log scale; the dashed line
is P/D = 1. In semi-enclosed seas a rising P/D has been linked to nutrient enrichment; in open
areas it mostly follows what the fleets target.

*What it shows for area 67.* P/D fell from `r round(pd$decades$pd_mean[1], 2)` in the
`r pd$decades$period[1]` to `r round(pd$decades$pd_mean[nrow(pd$decades)], 3)` in the
`r pd$decades$period[nrow(pd$decades)]`. It does not mean the sea lost its nutrients: the herring
fisheries shrank while the trawl fisheries for groundfish grew, so the ratio tells the history of
the fishery.

### 9.5 A distant-water fleet: `distant_water_profile()`

```{r, figures = "distant_water"}
japan_dw <- distant_water_profile("Japan")
```

🔎 *How to read them.* The catch of one country in the FAO areas it borders ("adjacent") and in
the others ("distant-water"), the share of distant-water catch, the number of areas fished each
year and when it entered each area (Swartz et al. 2010).

```{r, include = FALSE}
dw <- japan_dw$yearly[order(japan_dw$yearly$Year), ]
dw_peak <- dw[which.max(dw$distant_pct), ]
dw_last <- dw[dw$Year == max(dw$Year), ]
jp67_peak <- japan[as.character(dw_peak$Year)]
```

*What it shows.* Japan's only adjacent area is area 61. Its distant-water share rose to
`r pct(dw_peak$distant_pct)` in `r dw_peak$Year`, when it fished `r dw_peak$n_distant_areas`
distant FAO areas; in that year area 67 alone gave `r mt(jp67_peak, 2)`, or
`r pct(100 * jp67_peak / dw_peak$distant_tonnes, 0)` of its distant-water catch. The 200-mile
zones of the late 1970s closed the richest of these waters, and the share was
`r pct(dw_last$distant_pct)` in `r dw_last$Year`. Area 67 and Japan show the two sides of the same
change.

## 10. 🌡️ Species traits and temperature {#temperature}

### 10.1 FishBase traits: `fishbase_match()`

```{r}
traits <- fishbase_match(area67, version = "builtin")
show_table(traits[, c("species_en", "catch_pct", "match_type", "trophic_level", "temp_pref_mean")], n = 8)
```

🔎 *How to read it.* Each FAO species item is matched to FishBase or SeaLifeBase by published rules
(exact name, synonym, WoRMS, the mean of a higher taxon); `match_type` says which rule was used and
each row has links to check it. `version = "builtin"` uses the table bundled with the package, so
it works offline. Matches are first guesses: check the main ones with the links (see
[🐠 FishBase](fishbase.html)).

### 10.2 Sea surface temperature and the mean temperature of the catch

```{r, figures = "mtc"}
sst67 <- fao_area_sst("Pacific, Northeast")
mtc <- mean_temperature_catch(area67, version = "builtin")
show_table(mtc$trend[, c("period_start", "period_end", "mtc_slope_per_decade", "trend", "sst_slope_per_decade", "cor_mtc_sst")])
```

🔎 *How to read it.* The **mean temperature of the catch** (MTC, red) is the average preferred
temperature of the species caught, weighted by their catch (Cheung et al. 2013); the blue line is
the sea surface temperature (SST) of the area and the light band its range within the area. The
lower panel is the share of the catch with a known preferred temperature; years below 50% are
faded. A rising MTC means warm-water species take a larger share of the catch.

```{r, include = FALSE}
my <- mtc$yearly[!is.na(mtc$yearly$mtc) & !mtc$yearly$low_coverage, ]
low <- my[which.min(my$mtc), ]
high <- my[which.max(my$mtc), ]
last_mtc <- my[nrow(my), ]
pref <- function(name) round(mtc$species$temp_pref_mean[match(name, mtc$species$species_en)], 1)
pol_low <- 100 * sum(area67$Production[area67$Year == low$year & area67$ASFIS.species..Name. == pollock_name]) /
  sum(area67$Production[area67$Year == low$year])
tr <- mtc$trend
```

*What it shows for area 67.* The MTC stays between `r round(low$mtc, 1)` and
`r round(high$mtc, 1)` °C, far below the SST of the area (`r round(last_mtc$sst_mean, 1)` °C in
`r last_mtc$year`). The reason is the species: the main catch is of cold-water fishes that live
near the bottom, such as the pollock (preferred temperature `r pref(pollock_name)` °C) and the
Pacific cod (`r pref("Pacific cod")` °C). The MTC was lowest in `r low$year`, when the pollock gave
`r pct(pol_low, 0)` of the catch, and highest in `r high$year`, before the pollock fishery grew;
the Pacific hake of the US west coast (`r pref("North Pacific hake")` °C) raises it in the years
when its catch is large. The trend of the MTC is "`r tr$trend[1]`" over
`r tr$period_start[1]`–`r tr$period_end[1]` (`r round(tr$mtc_slope_per_decade[1], 3)` °C per decade) and
"`r tr$trend[2]`" over `r tr$period_start[2]`–`r tr$period_end[2]` (`r round(tr$mtc_slope_per_decade[2], 3)` °C per decade) while the
SST warmed by `r round(tr$sst_slope_per_decade[2], 2)` °C per decade. The MTC of area 67 follows
the mix of target species more than the ocean: read it with the species charts.

## 11. 📉 Stock assessment of the main species {#cmsy}

`cmsy_area()` runs the CMSY++ catch-only stock assessment (Froese et al. 2023) for the species
with the largest catch. It needs the JAGS program once (`cmsy_setup()`, see
[📉 CMSY++](cmsy.html)) and takes a few minutes; the charts below were made beforehand with the
same code.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
cmsy_setup()                                            # once: JAGS and the R packages
nep_cmsy <- cmsy_area("Pacific, Northeast", top = 10)   # the ten main species
nep_cmsy$summary                                        # B/Bmsy, F/Fmsy, MSY, status
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
cmsy_summary <- utils::read.csv(file.path(fig_dir, "cmsy_summary.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
show_png("kobe_all.png")
```

🔎 *How to read the Kobe plot.* Each circle is one stock in its last year: its biomass relative to
the biomass that gives the maximum sustainable yield (B/Bmsy, horizontal) and its fishing
pressure relative to the one that gives it (F/Fmsy, vertical); the size is the catch. Green
(bottom right): healthy; red (top left): overfished and still overfishing; orange and yellow:
one of the two. The dashed line at B/Bmsy = 0.8 separates "maximally sustainably fished" from
"overfished" in the FAO classes for catch-only results.

*What it shows for area 67.* `r sum(cmsy_summary$B_Bmsy < 0.8, na.rm = TRUE)` of the
`r nrow(cmsy_summary)` stocks assessed were below 0.8 Bmsy in their last year; the lowest were
`r paste0(cmsy_summary$species[order(cmsy_summary$B_Bmsy)][1:2], " (", cmsy_summary$B_Bmsy[order(cmsy_summary$B_Bmsy)][1:2], ")", collapse = " and ")`,
the two fisheries whose catch has fallen furthest from its peak.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
show_table(cmsy_summary[, intersect(names(cmsy_summary), c("Stock", "species", "B_Bmsy", "F_Fmsy", "MSY", "status"))])
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
show_png("overview.png")
```

🔎 *How to read it.* One row per stock: its B/Bmsy in the last year with the 95% confidence limits
(the bar), coloured by status. A long bar means the data could not pin the stock size down.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
show_png("status_time.png")
```

🔎 *How to read it.* The share of the assessed stocks in each status class, year by year. It shows
whether the stocks of the area moved together, e.g. all declining in the same years.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
show_png("management_first.png")
```

🔎 *How to read it.* The "management" chart of the largest stock (`r cmsy_summary$species[1]`): the
catch with the MSY (top left), the fishing pressure F/Fmsy (top right), the biomass B/Bmsy with the
lines at Bmsy and 0.8 Bmsy (bottom left), and the path of the stock through the Kobe plot (bottom
right). Shaded bands are the 95% limits. See [📉 CMSY++](cmsy.html) for all CMSY++ charts.

::: callout-warning
FAO capture statistics have no abundance index, so these are **catch-only** assessments driven
largely by their priors: indicative only, never a replacement for a full stock assessment. This
matters in area 67: most of its main stocks are assessed every year by the fishery agencies of the
United States and Canada with survey data, and their catch is held by catch limits, so a catch that
stays below its old peak can be read by a catch-only method as a smaller stock. Compare these
results with the official assessments before using them. The CMSY++ code is that of its authors
(<https://github.com/SISTA16/cmsyPlusPlus>); see the disclaimer in [📉 CMSY++](cmsy.html).
:::

## 12. 📝 The report in Word, LaTeX and PDF {#report}

`fao_report()` runs the analyses of the area and writes the whole assessment as a report: cover,
abstract, data and methods, results with charts and tables, conclusions, references and
appendix. Here a Word report in English, with the catch shocks and the mean temperature of the
catch added to the default sections:

```{r}
report <- fao_report(67, lang = "en", shocks = TRUE, mtc = TRUE)
report
```

The headings of the Word file:

```{r}
doc <- officer::docx_summary(officer::read_docx(report$file[["docx"]]))
headings <- doc$text[doc$style_name %in% c("FAO Heading 1", "FAO Heading 2")]
headings
```

### 12.1 Before the PDF: install TinyTeX once {#tinytex}

The Word file and the LaTeX source (`format = "latex"`) need nothing else. The **PDF** is compiled
from the LaTeX source with XeLaTeX, which comes with a LaTeX distribution. The simplest is
[TinyTeX](https://yihui.org/tinytex/) (Xie 2019), a small distribution installed from R, without
administrator rights:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("tinytex")
tinytex::install_tinytex()   # once, a few minutes; restart R afterwards
tinytex::is_tinytex()        # TRUE when it is installed
```

The first PDF takes longer: TinyTeX downloads the LaTeX packages the report uses (e.g. `ctex` and
the Chinese fonts for a Chinese report) and keeps them for the next times. If TinyTeX was installed
long ago and the PDF fails with a message such as "TeX Live is older than remote", update it with
`tinytex::reinstall_tinytex()`. [📝 Assessment report](report.html#tinytex) lists the other cases
(another LaTeX distribution, compiling an edited `.tex` file).

### 12.2 The same report as LaTeX and PDF

The same report as LaTeX and PDF, in Chinese, with CMSY++ (reusing the results of step 11 so
CMSY++ does not run again):

```{r, eval = FALSE}
fao_report(67, lang = "zh", format = c("docx", "latex", "pdf"), shocks = TRUE, mtc = TRUE,
           cmsy = nep_cmsy)
```

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `reports/FAO67_report_en.docx` | The Word report, to edit and complete |
| `reports/FAO67_report_zh.tex` and `reports/FAO67_report_zh_figures/` | The LaTeX source and its figures |
| `reports/FAO67_report_zh.pdf` | The PDF (needs XeLaTeX, e.g. TinyTeX, see [above](#tinytex)) |

::: callout-note
The report is a **first draft**: the text is written from templates filled with the results. Read
it, complete the grey "To be completed" notes (other data sources, discussion, other references)
and check every conclusion against the charts above. See
[📝 Assessment report](report.html) for every option.
:::

## 13. 🗂️ Where everything is saved and how to get it back {#files}

Every function writes into the working directory:

| Folder | What | Written by |
|---|---|---|
| `figures/png/` | `fishing_trend.png`, `fishing_percentage.png` | `fishing_area_data()` |
| `figures/png/area/` | `area_species*.png`, `area_country*.png` | `fishing_area_species()`, `fishing_area_country()` |
| `figures/png/` | `area_country_map.png`, `<species>_country_map.png` | maps of `fishing_area_country()`, `species_country()` |
| `figures/png/species/` | `<species>_country_*.png` | `species_country()` |
| `figures/png/country/` | `<country>_species_*.png`, `<country>analysis_*.png`, `<country>yearly_area_production*.png` | `country_species()`, `country_analysis()` |
| `figures/png/summary/` | `<label>_<analysis>*.png`, e.g. `Pacific__Northeast_stock_status_stocks.png` | the summary and literature analyses |
| `figures/pptx/...` | The same charts as PowerPoint files | when `pptx = TRUE` |
| `tables/` | CSV tables (UTF-8, open in Excel) | every function with `table = TRUE` |
| `reports/` | The reports, and `reports/cmsy/` with the CMSY++ results | `fao_report()` |
| `cmsy_areas/` | The CMSY++ runs, charts and tables of each area | `cmsy_area()` |

The files saved by this tutorial:

```{r}
head(list.files("figures/png", recursive = TRUE), 20)
length(list.files("figures/png", recursive = TRUE))
head(list.files("tables"), 10)
```

**Getting results back.** Every function also returns its results to R (assign them, as above).
To continue another day, save them and read them back, or read the CSV tables:

```{r}
saveRDS(list(NEP = NEP, status = status, mtc = mtc), "area67_results.rds")
results <- readRDS("area67_results.rds")
names(results)
head(read.csv("tables/Pacific__Northeast_stock_status_stocks.csv"), 3)
```

When FAO publishes a new release, run `download_fao_data()` and the same code again: every chart,
table and number is recomputed from the new data, and `fao_data_info()` gives the new citation.

## 14. 🎨 Make it yours

The same analyses in Chinese or bilingual charts, another style or map projection:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
fao_settings(lang = "zh")                  # Chinese charts and names
fao_settings(lang = "both")                # Chinese and English on the same chart
fao_settings(theme = "minimal", palette = "npg", map_projection = "robinson", map_center = 180)
fao_settings(reset = TRUE)                 # back to the defaults
```

See [🎨 Customise charts and maps](customise.html) for all settings.

## ✅ Summary

| Step | Function | Main output |
|---|---|---|
| Data | `load_fao_data()`, `fao_data_info()` | The data and the release to cite |
| Area | `fishing_area_data()` | Total catch, stages, share of the world |
| Species, countries | `fishing_area_species()`, `fishing_area_country()`, `species_country()`, `country_species()`, `country_analysis()` | Who catches what, and its stages |
| Status | `species_group_composition()`, `stock_status()`, `peak_trend()`, `regime_shift()`, `area_overview()` | Composition, status, trends, shifts |
| Quality, fleets | `data_quality()`, `diversity_concentration()`, `country_group_summary()`, `coastal_distant()` | How reliable and how concentrated |
| Literature | `catch_shocks()`, `collapse_analysis()`, `catch_synchrony()`, `pelagic_demersal()`, `distant_water_profile()` | Shocks, collapses, synchrony, P/D, fleets |
| Temperature | `fishbase_match()`, `fao_area_sst()`, `mean_temperature_catch()` | Traits, SST, MTC |
| Assessment | `cmsy_area()` | B/Bmsy, F/Fmsy, MSY |
| Report | `fao_report()`, with TinyTeX for the PDF | Word, LaTeX, PDF |
